description: Equipo "AstroNova.CO" de la Escuela Técnica Austral de Petroleros Jerárquicos
summary:
Echoes of Space

Our project was developed by 'AstroNova.CO', a team representing Escuela Técnica Austral, Argentina, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Our mission is to bring the stories of NASA's abandoned space equipment to life, demonstrating how their scientific legacy continues to inspire future generations.

Using official NASA resources, particularly the NSSDCA, we developed two complementary educational platforms.

NASA Mission Atlas offers detailed scientific information, interactive 3D exploration, mission comparisons and quizzes for teenagers and adults. Space Atlas provides a simpler, visual experience for children, allowing them to discover spacecraft histories through interactive models.

We also developed Echoes of Space, browser-based 3D educational games featuring lunar and Martian exploration, historical missions, scientific challenges and decisions with consequences.

Using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js and AI-assisted development tools, we transformed historical mission records into engaging learning experiences.

Our goal is to make space science accessible, encourage curiosity and inspire interest in astronomy, engineering and exploration.

Their missions ended, but their legacy continues.
details:
1. Project Overview

NASA Mission Atlas and Space Atlas are complementary educational platforms developed by AstroNova.CO, a team representing Escuela Técnica Austral, Argentina, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Together with our interactive educational games, Echoes of Space, these platforms form a project designed to preserve and share the stories of NASA's historic space equipment.

Our project responds to the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars".

Our main objective is to bring the stories of historic spacecraft, rovers, landers, satellites and scientific instruments to new generations, highlighting their technological achievements and scientific contributions.

We wanted to demonstrate that even when space equipment stops operating, its scientific legacy continues to contribute to humanity's understanding of the Universe.

To achieve this, we combined scientific research, interactive 3D exploration, historical storytelling, programming and game-based learning.

Rather than simply presenting information about abandoned spacecraft, we developed educational experiences that allow visitors to explore their stories, interact with virtual environments and learn through discovery.

2. How Does Our Project Work?

Our project begins with an introductory screen featuring the school's logo, our team name and the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

From this screen, visitors can select between two educational experiences: a basic level or an advanced level.

The introductory visual was created with the assistance of artificial intelligence, which we have identified in our AI usage disclosure.

This structure allows users to choose an experience according to their age, interests and previous knowledge.

Basic Level – Space Atlas

Space Atlas was developed using Base44 and is designed primarily for children and younger audiences.

It introduces NASA's historic missions through colourful visual elements, simplified scientific explanations and interactive exploration.

One of its main features is a three-dimensional explorer displaying representations of historic spacecraft and scientific instruments.

Visitors can rotate the scene, zoom in and select individual objects. When an object is selected, information about its history, original mission and scientific contributions becomes available.

This approach encourages children to explore independently, transforming historical information into a visual discovery experience.

The platform also provides access to our independently developed educational games, Echoes of Space, where visitors can experience interactive adventures inspired by NASA's historic missions.

Advanced Level – NASA Mission Atlas

NASA Mission Atlas was developed using Lovable and is designed for teenagers and adults who wish to explore the scientific information in greater detail.

The platform includes an interactive 3D explorer, mission categories, search tools, filters, visual discovery resources, mission comparisons, educational statistics and quizzes.

Visitors can examine historic spacecraft and compare information such as mission dates, locations, equipment mass, categories and operational status, where verified information is available.

The platform also includes an educational orbital simulator demonstrating how orbital altitude affects speed and period under simplified conditions.

The knowledge quiz allows visitors to evaluate what they have learnt through interactive questions.

Both platforms present a catalogue of 13 thematic records covering historic NASA spacecraft, scientific instruments and mission groups.

Some records correspond to individual spacecraft, while others represent related missions or collections of equipment.

By providing two educational levels, we aim to make the same scientific knowledge accessible to users with different learning needs.

3. Echoes of Space – Interactive Educational Games

In addition to the two educational platforms, our team developed Echoes of Space, a collection of browser-based 3D exploration experiences inspired by historic NASA missions.

The games combine simulated environments, interactive storytelling, educational questions, exploration objectives and decisions with consequences.

Players do not simply read about historic spacecraft. They participate in simulated missions designed to introduce their scientific achievements and the challenges of space exploration.

Lunar Exploration

Our lunar experience allows players to explore educational simulations inspired by historic equipment left on the Moon.

It features missions involving:

  • Apollo 11: Exploring the area surrounding the Eagle lunar module and discovering the history of the first human Moon landing.
  • Lunar Roving Vehicles: Learning about the electric vehicles used during Apollo 15, 16 and 17.
  • ALSEP Scientific Instruments: Discovering the scientific equipment installed by Apollo astronauts to continue collecting information after their departure.
  • Surveyor 3: Exploring the history of the robotic lander that helped prepare the way for subsequent lunar exploration.

Players can control astronauts and lunar vehicles, follow simulated routes, discover scientific information and complete mission-specific tasks.

The experience incorporates interactive navigation, mission briefings, scientific records, minimaps, checkpoints, educational quizzes and scoring systems.

A mission log allows players to review their progress and revisit information discovered during exploration.

Resource indicators represent factors such as energy, equipment integrity and communications.

Decisions made during the missions can influence the player's resources and progression.

Mars and Deep-Space Exploration

Our second game environment focuses on Mars and other historic NASA exploration missions.

It includes ten educational campaigns featuring Spirit, Opportunity, Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Phoenix and InSight, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, Ingenuity and Kepler.

Each campaign introduces the historical context of the mission, its scientific objectives and the discoveries it made possible.

One example is Opportunity: The Last Signal, in which players control a robotic rover navigating a simulated Martian landscape.

Players follow routes marked by checkpoints, avoid obstacles, investigate scientific points of interest and make decisions that affect their available resources.

The game includes detailed terrain, mountains, craters, rocks, environmental effects and changing conditions.

Players can encounter dust storms, wind and temperature variations, as well as fictional events designed to make exploration more engaging.

Additional gameplay features allow an astronaut character to explore the environment, walk, run, jump and recover mission-related objects or information.

The decisions encountered during the journey may have positive or negative consequences.

For example, collecting additional scientific information may require sacrificing energy, while choosing a safer route may preserve the vehicle's integrity.

We also introduced scoring systems, mission summaries and interactive educational activities.

For missions involving stationary landers, orbiters, helicopters or deep-space spacecraft, we adapted the activities to their historical characteristics.

Some routes represent symbolic navigation or scientific observation rather than actual spacecraft movement.

This allows visitors to learn about different types of exploration equipment without incorrectly representing how they operated.

Both game experiences support Spanish and English, allowing a broader audience to access the educational content.

4. Scientific Research and NASA Resources

Scientific accuracy was a central priority throughout our project.

Following the official resources provided for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we used the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) as a central source for our historical and scientific research.

We also used official NASA Science and NASA/JPL mission information to complement the research and support the educational content.

Our project covers all thirteen thematic groups of missions and equipment highlighted in the challenge's resource list.

These include Apollo lunar modules, Lunar Roving Vehicles, ALSEP scientific instruments, Surveyor landers, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Viking, Phoenix and InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer and Kepler.

We researched the purpose of each spacecraft, its development, mission objectives, operational history and scientific achievements.

This information forms the educational foundation of our websites and interactive experiences.

In the games, players encounter scientific facts, historical questions and challenges connected to the equipment featured in NASA's records.

The objective is not simply to memorise information, but to understand why these missions were important and how their discoveries contributed to scientific progress.

We adapted the complexity of this information to different age groups while preserving the historical context.

We also distinguished authentic scientific information from fictional gameplay elements.

The simulated routes, resource indicators, scores, environmental events and player decisions are educational mechanics. They do not represent actual historical events, mission telemetry or spacecraft operations.

This distinction allows us to combine creative storytelling with responsible scientific communication.

5. Development Process: From a Simple Prototype to Interactive Games

Our development process was based on continuous experimentation, testing and improvement.

The project did not begin as a complete video game.

Our first prototype consisted of a simple three-dimensional sphere representing Mars.

We subsequently introduced interactive points of interest displaying information about historic NASA missions.

As we explored the possibilities of the 3D environment, we decided to transform the visualisation into a playable educational experience.

The initial movement prototype consisted of a basic arrow that could rotate around its own axis.

We later replaced it with a robotic rover that players could control using their keyboard.

We progressively introduced rocks, obstacles, navigation routes and checkpoints.

At these checkpoints, we added educational activities connected to the history of abandoned spacecraft.

The experience gradually evolved into a game incorporating role-playing mechanics, where different decisions produced positive or negative consequences.

Players could gain scientific information while consuming energy or make alternative choices affecting their resources.

As development continued, we improved the environment by introducing terrain textures, mountains, craters, environmental effects and changing conditions.

We also developed astronaut movement, including walking, running and jumping, together with additional exploration objectives.

Further improvements included interactive maps, mission briefings, scoring systems, scientific records, music and sound effects.

To make the experience more enjoyable and encourage exploration, we introduced optional fictional Easter eggs, including meteor showers and humorous narrative sequences.

These features were introduced progressively rather than all at once.

Each version helped us identify new possibilities, improve existing mechanics and refine the educational experience.

Development eventually expanded to include lunar exploration experiences inspired by Apollo, ALSEP, LRV and Surveyor missions.

What began as a simple representation of Mars became a collection of interactive educational experiences combining scientific storytelling, exploration and decision-making.

6. Testing, Debugging and Problem-Solving

Testing was an essential part of our development methodology.

After implementing each new feature, we tested the game to verify its functionality, identify limitations and detect programming errors.

Whenever a problem occurred, we investigated its possible causes before attempting to correct it.

One particularly challenging situation occurred when the rover reached a critically low condition.

The intended behaviour was for the vehicle to stop and undergo repairs. However, a programming error caused the application to stop functioning.

To recover a stable version, we had to revert to a version saved three iterations earlier, losing some of our most recent improvements.

Other difficulties involved collision detection, obstacles interfering with navigation, route design and errors that prevented certain files from opening correctly.

These problems required repeated testing, code corrections and adjustments.

We used Claude Code to assist with programming and debugging, while our team evaluated the results and decided which changes were necessary.

This process taught us the importance of maintaining stable versions, identifying errors systematically and understanding how modifications can affect existing functionality.

Our development followed a continuous cycle:

Prototype → Test → Identify Problems → Investigate → Correct → Improve → Test Again

Rather than treating errors as the end of development, we used them as opportunities to improve the project.

This iterative approach was fundamental in transforming our initial concept into functional educational experiences.

7. Tools, Programming Languages and Technologies

Our team combined traditional web programming, 3D graphics technologies, development software and artificial intelligence tools.

Programming Languages and Technologies

HTML5

Used to structure the interactive games, navigation menus, mission information, buttons and educational interfaces.

CSS3

Used to design the visual interface, panels, resource indicators, animations and responsive layouts.

JavaScript (ES6+)

Used to implement gameplay mechanics, rover and astronaut movement, mission progression, resource management, scoring systems, decisions and user interactions.

Three.js

Used to develop the three-dimensional environments, spacecraft representations, rover models, cameras, lighting, terrain, animations and interactive scenes.

WebGL

Used through Three.js to render three-dimensional graphics directly in compatible web browsers.

Development Software and AI Tools

Visual Studio Code

Our primary development environment for programming, editing, testing and improving the interactive games.

Claude Code

Used as an AI-assisted programming tool to support code development, debugging, graphical improvements, sound integration and the implementation of additional features.

Lovable

Used to develop NASA Mission Atlas, our advanced educational platform.

Base44

Used to develop Space Atlas, our basic educational platform, and provide access to the interactive games.

Google Gemini

Used to assist in developing the educational quizzes.

ChatGPT

Used to support documentation, writing, editing, translation and the organisation of project information.

Scientific Resources

NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA)

Used as a central scientific and historical research resource.

NASA Science and NASA/JPL

Used as additional official sources for spacecraft histories, mission objectives and scientific achievements.

Our project was developed primarily using computers and web-based technologies, without requiring specialised hardware for visitors.

The interactive experiences run through compatible web browsers, reducing the need for additional software installations.

Artificial intelligence supported our development process, while our team defined the educational objectives, selected the scientific content, guided the design, tested the results and directed the improvements.

8. Creativity and Innovation

Our project's creativity lies in transforming historical NASA mission records into interactive educational experiences adapted to different audiences.

Instead of presenting abandoned spacecraft as a static collection of technical information, we created environments that allow visitors to discover their stories through interaction and exploration.

The project combines three complementary approaches.

Scientific Discovery

Visitors can examine spacecraft, select interactive objects and access information about their history and scientific achievements.

Interactive Exploration

Players can explore simulated lunar and Martian environments, control vehicles and astronauts, complete objectives and discover scientific information.

Decision-Based Learning

Players encounter situations requiring choices. Their decisions affect resources and progression, encouraging them to consider the challenges involved in planning and managing space exploration activities.

Another distinctive feature is the separation between basic and advanced educational experiences.

Younger audiences can discover missions through simplified information and visual interaction, while older visitors can access more detailed scientific content and comparisons.

The games reinforce these experiences by transforming historical information into interactive challenges.

We also incorporated optional fictional events and creative details to encourage exploration, while ensuring that historical facts remain distinguishable from gameplay elements.

Our use of AI-assisted development tools allowed us to experiment with new ideas and progressively improve the project.

However, the educational direction, creative decisions, testing and problem-solving remained guided by our team.

We believe this combination of scientific research, programming, artificial intelligence and creativity demonstrates how technology can make space education more accessible and engaging.

9. Design Considerations

Several factors influenced our development decisions.

Scientific Accuracy

We prioritised official NASA information and distinguished verified historical facts from fictional educational simulations.

Educational Accessibility

We adapted the complexity of the explanations and visual presentation to different age groups.

Interactive Learning

We wanted users to participate actively in discovering scientific information rather than relying exclusively on traditional reading.

Ease of Access

We developed browser-based experiences to reduce the need for additional software or specialised equipment.

Technical Performance

We considered graphical performance, navigation, collision detection, controls and application stability throughout development.

Language Accessibility

We incorporated Spanish and English language options into the exploration games to reach a broader audience.

Educational and Entertainment Balance

We introduced interactive mechanics and creative elements to maintain user interest while preserving the scientific objectives.

Continuous Improvement

We progressively refined the project through testing, debugging, experimentation and evaluation of new features.

10. Benefits and Intended Impact

Our primary objective is to encourage children, teenagers and adults to discover the history of NASA's space exploration missions.

We want visitors to understand how spacecraft were developed, why they were sent into space, what scientific discoveries they made possible and what happened after their missions ended.

Through our platforms, users can explore historic equipment, examine scientific information and discover the technological achievements behind different missions.

Through our games, players can participate in simulated exploration activities, answer historical questions and make decisions that affect their progress.

This combination promotes active learning, curiosity and problem-solving.

We hope to encourage greater interest in astronomy, engineering, robotics, programming and scientific research, particularly among younger generations.

The project is also intended to serve as an educational resource for schools, science outreach activities and independent learning.

We believe that combining scientific information with interactive technologies can help make complex subjects more approachable and engaging.

Another intended impact is to demonstrate how students and educators can use modern programming tools and artificial intelligence responsibly to create meaningful educational experiences.

Ultimately, we want visitors to recognise that the equipment left behind during space exploration represents much more than abandoned machinery.

These spacecraft and instruments helped expand our scientific knowledge and remain an important part of humanity's exploration history.

11. Conclusion

NASA Mission Atlas, Space Atlas and Echoes of Space represent the work of AstroNova.CO to transform NASA's historical mission records into accessible and interactive educational experiences.

Using official NASA scientific resources, we developed two complementary websites and interactive exploration games featuring historic missions to the Moon, Mars and other destinations throughout the Solar System.

Our development process involved experimentation, successive prototypes, technical challenges, programming corrections and continuous improvements.

By combining HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Three.js, WebGL and AI-assisted development tools, we created experiences that connect science, technology, history and storytelling.

Above all, our project demonstrates that historic spacecraft and scientific instruments are not simply forgotten machines.

They represent human ingenuity, technological progress and discoveries that continue to shape our understanding of the Universe.

By making their stories accessible through interactive education, we hope to inspire future generations of scientists, engineers and explorers.

Their missions ended, but their legacy continues.
